unitdesc: HARMONY FORMATION (Upper Cambrian)-Feldspathic and arkosic sandstone and minor amounts of shale, limestone, and chert.
strat_unit: Paradise Valley Chert
unit_com: Stewart and McKee, 1977, describe the Harmony Formation in northern Lander County as mostly feldspathic sandstone and arkose with shale and calcareous shale and small amounts of pebbly sandstone and limestone. Willden, 1964, describes the Harmony Formation in southern Humboldt County as feldspathic graywacke and feldspathic quartzite with lesser amounts of sandy limestone, calcareous graywacke, feldspathic pebble conglomerate, and shale, as well as altered volcanic rocks near the Hot Springs Range (altered diabase and greenstone). These volcanic rocks are so rare in the unit as a whole that I have chosen not to include them in the lithology coding. The Paradise Valley Chert is 300 to 500 feet thick with no exposed base; the Harmony Formation is hesitantly estimated at 4000 to 5000+ feet thick (Willden, 1964). The Harmony Formation has been assigned to the transitional assemblage by other workers, but is thrust over the siliceous assemblage (Stewart and McKee, 1977).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV005 NV012 NV018

unitdesc: SCOTT CANYON FORMATION (Lower or Middle Cambrian)-Chert, shale, greenstone, and sparse limestone and quartzite. Southeast Humboldt County and northwest Lander County.
unit_com: The Scott Canyon Formation is about 5,000 feet thick (Stewart and McKee, 1977).This unit may be better included in the Transitional assemblage because this province contains lithologically similar archeocyanid and trilobite-bearing limestone (Stewart, 1980). Does not appear to outcrop in Humboldt County despite description (in either the state map or the county map).

unitdesc: SANDSTONE AND QUARTZITE-Includes Tapeats Sandstone and related rocks. Rests on Precambrian metamorphic rocks.
unit_com: The outcrops just north of the Clark County line are similar in lithology to the Prospect Mountain Quartzite (see unit NVCZq) and some geologists have referred to the sandstone unit in Clark County as such; "Tapeats Sandstone" was borrowed from a similar unit on the Colorado Plateau. In Nevada, this unit is 150-500 feet thick (Longwell and others, 1965).

unit_name: Shale and thin-bedded or laminated limestone; also thinly interbedded limestone and chert
unitdesc: SHALE AND THIN-BEDDED OR LAMINATED LIMESTONE; ALSO THINLY INTERBEDDED LIMESTONE AND CHERT-Includes units such as Preble and Emigrant Formations
strat_unit: Preble Formation, Emigrant Formation, Crane Canyon Sequence (in Lander County), Shwin Formation, Swarbrick Formation, Tybo (Dunderberg) Shale (in part), Hales Limestone (in part), Broad Canyon Formation (in small part), Tennessee Mountain Formation (in part)
unit_com: Shwin Formation contains the only volcanic rocks in the Middle and Upper Cambrian sequence (Stewart, 1980); these rocks include greenstone and phyllite derived from dolerite (diabase) (Stewart and McKee, 1977). The Tybo Shale has been reassigned to the Dunderberg Shale and the term abandoned (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985); the shale is mapped within this unit although the rest of the Dunderberg Shale is mapped within unit NVCc. Exposed sections of the Preble indicate 5,000 feet thickness but geologists have estimated 12,000 to 15,000 feet (Willden, 1964). The Emigrant Formation is at least 1,500 to 2,000 feet (Albers and Stewart, 1972). The Crane Canyon Formation is considered to be several thousand feet thick (Stewart and McKee, 1977). In Elko County, includes small outcrop of undifferentiated strata mapped primarily in NVCc (Coats, 1987).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV005 NV009 NV013

unit_name: Quartzite and minor amounts of conglomerate, phyllitic siltstone, limestone, and dolomite
unitdesc: QUARTZITE AND MINOR AMOUNTS OF CONGLOMERATE, PHYLLITIC SILTSTONE, LIMESTONE, AND DOLOMITE-Includes Prospect Mountain Quartzite, Osgood Mountain Quartzite, and Gold Hill Formation in northern Nevada, and Stirling Quartzite, Wood Canyon Formation, and Zabriskie Quartzite in southern Nevada.
strat_unit: Stella Lake Quartzite (part of McCoy Creek Group)
unit_com: Estimated range of thickness for the Prospect Mountain Quartzite in Elko County is 1,500 to 4,000 feet (Coats, 1987); in White Pine County, thickness is estimated at 4,500 feet (Hose and Blake, 1976). Estimated exposed thickness for Osgood Mountain Quartzite is 5,000 feet (Willden, 1964). In stratigraphic order, oldest to youngest, the Stirling Quartzite is almost complete at 5,300 feet thick; the Wood Canyon Formation is 2,100 feet thick; the Zabriskie Formation is 1,150 feet thick (Cornwall, 1972). The Daylight Formation and the Corkscrew Formation of Bare Mountain have been correlated with the Wood Canyon Formation and the Zabriskie Quartzite, respectively and both terms abandoned (Cornwall, 1972).
rocktype3: dolostone (dolomite); limestone; phyllite; shale; conglomerate; sandstone

unit_com: In stratigraphic order, oldest to youngest: the Reed Dolomite is 1,560 feet thick; the Deep Spring Formation is 1,500 feet thick; the Campito Formation is 2,500(?) feet thick; the Poleta Formation is 1000+ feet thick; the Harkless Formation (including Saline Valley Formation at the top) is 3,500 feet thick; the Mule Spring Limestone is 400-500 feet thick (main part of Esmeralda County, Albers and Stewart, 1972). Often lithologically similar, these formations can be separated by their respective fossils.

unitdesc: BANBURY FORMATION-Basalt, gravel, and tuffaceous sediments locally. Northeast Humboldt County and northwest Elko County

unit_name: Dolomite, limestone, and minor amounts of sandstone and quartzite
unitdesc: DOLOMITE, LIMESTONE, AND MINOR AMOUNTS OF SANDSTONE AND QUARTZITE-Includes units such as Sevy and Simonson Dolomites, Guilmette and Nevada Formations, and Devils Gate Limestone.
strat_unit: Wenban Limestone (equivalent to the Nevada Formation and Devils Gate Limestone), Pilot Shale (in part), Rabbit Hill Limestone, McMonnigal Limestone, Tor Limestone, Sultan Limestone, Muddy Peak Limestone
unit_com: The Nevada Formation has been divided into other formations by some geologists and the term is now considered obsolete by the U.S. Geological Survey (Coats, 1987). Other geologists consider the Nevada Formation to be equivalent to the Sevy Dolomite and the Simonson Dolomite (Hose and Blake, 1976) and Guilmette Formation (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). About 65-75% of the Simonson is dolomite while the remaining portion is orthoquartzite and limestone; the thickness ranges from 500 to 1800 feet. The Guilmette is almost 70% limestone while the remaining portion is mostly dolostone; the thickness is 1050-2500 feet thick. The Sevy Formation is 1,300 feet thick and primarily dolostone with some cherty beds and some sandstone (Coats, 1987, Hose and Blake, 1976). In Eureka, the Devonian strata (Rabbit Hill Limestone, Nevada Formation, Devil's Gate Limestone, and Pilot Shale) is primarily limestone with lesser dolomite, shale, and sandstone. Note that the proportions of dolostone to limestone in the Nevada Formation vary east to west (Roberts and others, 1967). The proportions of dolostone to limestone in the Guilmette Formation appear to vary geographically as well with increasing limestone westward and increasing dolostone east and southward (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). The Sultan and Muddy Peak Limestone occur in Clark County of which the upper part is mostly limestone and the lower is mostly dolostone (Longwell and others, 1965).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV003 NV007 NV008 NV010 NV011 NV013

unitdesc: DOLOMITE AND LIMESTONE (Lower Paleozoic)
unit_com: Limited to outcrops in Lincoln and Elko Counties. In Lincoln County, includes undifferentiated dolostone and limestone, of Cambrian through Devonian age (Tschanz and Pampeyan, 1970). In Elko County, includes dolomite marble and lesser calcite marble as well as minor recrystallized chert and quartzite, questionably of Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, or Devonian age (Coats, 1987).

unit_name: Chert, shale, argillite, siltstone, quartzite, and greenstone
unitdesc: CHERT, SHALE, ARGILLITE, SILTSTONE, QUARTZITE, AND GREENSTONE-Undivided siliceous assemblage. Mostly Ordovician
unit_com: Limited to Snake Mountains of Elko County where chert, orthoquartzite, and limestone in the north grade to chert conglomerate and siltstone in the south, relative amounts unreported (Coats, 1987). No greenstone mentioned. Maybe Valmy and Vinini Formations.

unit_name: Shale, siliceous siltstone, chert, and minor amounts of limestone
unitdesc: SHALE, SILICEOUS SILTSTONE, CHERT, AND MINOR AMOUNTS OF LIMESTONE-Includes Cockalorum Wash Formation of northern Nye County and Woodruff Formation and unnamed rocks in Elko County
unit_com: The Cockalorum Wash Formation is 1,200 feet thick. Both the Cockalorum Wash and Woodruff Formations host eurypetid claws (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). The Cockalorum Wash type section has 600 feet of shale, platy siltstone, and sandstone with limestone lenses and interbeds and 500 feet of limestone (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985); the Woodruff Formation in southern Elko County is 500 to 600 feet of shale overlain by 700 to 800 feet of chert with limestone occurring as a minor constituent; total thickness throughout the County can be over 3000 feet (Coats, 1987).

unitdesc: SLAVEN CHERT-Chert and sparse limy sandstone, siltstone, and limestone. Lander County
unit_com: Outcrops in northern Nye County possibly correlative with Slaven Chert; includes "notable baritic zones" (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). Estimated thickness of the Slaven Chert is between 2000 to 4000 feet (Stewart and McKee, 1977).

unitdesc: ARGILLACEOUS LIMESTONE, CHERT, AND SHALE-Elko and Eureka Counties
unit_com: Coats, 1987, includes calcareous siltstone in Elko County. In Eureka County, the few occurances include sandy and calcareous shale and sandstone. In general, these Devonian rocks are considered transitional because they contain more limestone and less chert than rocks of the siliceous western assemblage (Roberts and others, 1967).

unitdesc: DUNLAP FORMATION (Lower and Middle Jurassic)-Conglomerate, sandstone, greenstone, felsite, and tuff. Locally contemporaneous with folding and thrusting. Mineral County and adjacent parts of Esmeralda and Nye Counties
unit_com: The thickness of the Dunlap Formation ranges from 3,000 to 5,000 feet thick.

unitdesc: GABBROIC COMPLEX (Lower and Middle Jurassic)-Includes gabbro, basalt, and synorogenic quartz sandstone (Boyer Ranch Formation). Churchill and Pershing Counties
unit_com: The gabbro intrudes the quartz arenite and comagmatic basaltic rocks; intrusion and extrusion is likely contemporaneous with thrusting of the quartz arenite. The volcanic section is at least 1,700 feet thick (Willden and Speed, 1974); the thickness of the quartz arenite is 500 feet, of which the bottom 125 feet is dolomite conglomerate and 25 feet of limestone (Boyer Ranch Formation of Johnson, 1977). I estimate the ratio of gabbro to mafic volcanic rock to be around 2:1.

unit_name: Volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, tuff, andesite and felsitic flows, and carbonate rocks

strat_unit: Excelsior Formation (in Paradise Range and part of Pilot and Excelsior Mountains); Pablo Formation (in Paradise Range); Dunlap Formation (in part of Pilot and Excelsior Mountains)
unit_com: No outcrop in Esmeralda County. Outcrops part of stratigraphic units listed above in select areas. Vitaliano and Callaghan (1963) report large areas of greenstone and lesser amounts intermediate to silicic volcanic rocks in Paradise Peak Quadrangle.

unitdesc: AZTEC SANDSTONE (Triassic? And Jurassic)-Friable fine- to medium-grained sandstone with conspicuous large-scale cross strata; considered eolian. Age based on correlation with Navajo Sandstone
unit_com: Entirely in Clark County. The maximum exposed thickness of the unit is 2,000 to 2,500 feet (Longwell and others, 1965).

unit_com: In Humboldt and Pershing Counties, good portions of this unit have been metamorphosed to argillite, phyllite, quartzite, slate, and hornfels, schist, and gneissic rocks near intrusions (Willden, 1964, Johnson, 1977). The Nightingale Formation also includes some marble (Bonham, 1969). In Churchill County, this unit ranges from 5,000 to 20,000 feet thick (Willden and Speed, 1974); of the Auld Lang Syne Group, the Raspberry Formation ranges from 3,000 to 8,000 feet thick, the Winnemucca Formation ranges from 1,000 to 3,000 feet thick, the Grass Valley Formation ranges from 300 to 2,000 feet thick, the Dun Glen Formation is 1,150 feet thick, and the Osobb Formation is 1,800 feet thick (Willden, 1964, Johnson, 1977).

Most of the Peavine Sequence is metamorphosed, though greenschist facies upto amphibolite facies near intrusive contacts (Bonham, 1969); most of this unit in Lyon, Douglas and Ormsby Counties is at least partially metamorphosed as well (Moore, 1969).

unit_com: The area in the Dry Hills (~1/4 of the total area of this unit) is quartz latite; the area in the Cortez Mountains and southern Tuscarora Mountains is as described. The thickness of the unit in the Cortez Mountains and southern Tuscarora Mountains ranges from 3,500 to 10,000 feet thick (Robert and others, 1967).

unitdesc: GRANITIC ROCKS-Mostly quartz monzonite and granodiorite
unit_com: This unit is grouped with NVMzgr in the literature; the two units are the same types of rocks but those included in this unit have their ages confirmed by radiometric dating. Granodiorite is dominant over quartz monzonite in northern Nevada while the opposite is true in southern Nevada.

unit_age: Paleozoic sedimentary rocks with Mesozoic intrusive rocks
unitdesc: IGNEOUS AND METAMORPHIC COMPLEX-Pegmatitic granite and other granitic rocks complexly intermixed with metasedimentary rocks. Considered to be Mesozoic igneous complex intruding lower Paleozoic and possibly Precambrian Z sedimentary rocks. Grades into units shown on map as lower Paleozoic. Ruby Mountains and East Humboldt Range, Elko County
unit_com: This unit is almost entirely early and middle Paleozoic and late Proterozoic metamorphic rocks with a minor amount of Mesozoic gneiss and granitic rocks (Coats, 1987). Relative abundances of marble, schist, quartzite, and gneiss are generally unspecified in literature, especially for the Humboldt Range, though marble is dominant in the Ruby Mountains.
rocktype3: gneiss; quartzite; granulite; dolostone (dolomite); granite; pegmatite

unitdesc: CONTINENTAL DEPOSITS OF SILTSTONE, SHALE, CONGLOMERATE, AND LIMESTONE-Includes units such as King Lear Formation in Humboldt County, Newark Canyon Formation in Eureka County, Willow Tank Formation and baseline Sandstone in Clark County

unit_name: Limestone and minor amounts of dolomite and shale
unitdesc: LIMESTONE AND MINOR AMOUNTS OF DOLOMITE AND SHALE-Includes units such as Rogers Spring and Monte Cristo Limestones
unit_com: The Monte Cristo Limestone is typically divided into five members: the Dawn and Anchor Limestone (the latter with abundant chert), the Bullion Dolomite, and the Arrowhead and Yellowpine Limestone (Cornwall, 1972, Longwell and others, 1965).

unit_name: Conglomerate, limestone, meta-andesite, phyllite, and shale
unitdesc: CONGLOMERATE, LIMESTONE, META-ANDESITE, PHYLLITE, AND SHALE-Includes Grossman, Banner, Nelson, and Mountain City Formation. Northern Elko County
strat_unit: Diamond A Formation
unit_com: The Banner Formation is about 600 feet thick; the Nelson Formation ranges from 600 feet to possibly 2,500 feet thick; the Grossman is up to 2,000 feet thick. The Mountain City Formation lies conformably over the Nelson Formation but is possibly correlative with the Chainman Shale (see NVMDs) even though it is described here; it ranges from 4,000 feet thick to an estimated original thickness of 10,000 feet (Coats, 1987).
rocktype3: conglomerate; sandstone; siltstone; phyllite; limestone; diabase

unit_name: Sandy and silty limestone, conglomerate, and siltstone
unitdesc: SANDY AND SILTY LIMESTONE, CONGLOMERATE, AND SILTSTONE (Upper Pennsylvanian to Upper Permian)-Includes units such as Strathearn Formation of Dott (1955) and Buckskin Mountain, Beacon Flat, and Carlin Canyon Formations of Dott (1955)
strat_unit: Garden Valley Formation, Carbon Ridge Formation
unit_com: The Garden Valley Formation ranges from 2,700 to 5,000 feet thick (Roberts and others, 1967). Roberts and others, 1967 also reports that, in the Diamond Mountains, the Carbon Ridge Formation is 1,500 to 1,750 feet thick; Hose and Blake, 1976, report that it ranges from 1,400 to 2,300 feet thick. The Strathearn Formation ranges from 1,200 to 2,000 feet thick; the Buckskin Mountain Formation is about 1,200 feet thick; the Beacon Flat Formation is about 2,800 feet thick (Coats, 1987).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV007 NV008 NV010 NV013

unit_name: Shale, siltstone, sandstone, chert-pebble conglomerate, and limestone
unitdesc: SHALE, SILTSTONE, SANDSTONE, CHERT-PEBBLE CONGLOMERATE, AND LIMESTONE-Includes units such as Pilot Shale, Joana Limestone, Chainman Shale, and Diamond Peak Formation in northern and eastern Nevada and Narrow Canyon Limestone, Mercury Limestone, and Eleana Formation in southern Nevada
strat_unit: Bristol Pass Limestone, Tonka Formation, Sultan Limestone (in part), Scotty Wash Quartzite?
unit_com: The Pilot Shale, Joana Limestone, and Chainman Shale has been previously mapped as the White Pine Group (Hose and Blake, 1976). The stratigraphic units included in this map unit vary in relative abundances of lithologies as well as thicknesses, anywhere from less than one hundred feet to a few thousand feet. Generally the units located in the north thin southward and vice versa. Almost all of the units have some combination of all ofthe lithologies listed below. In southern Eureka County, there is an outcrop included in this unit which Roberts and others, 1967, maps as part of the Newark Canyon Formation, a unit of shale and sandstone with limestone and conglomerate of Early Cretaceous age; this unit is not included in the age coding below although it could be lithologically similar to the rest of this unit. The Elena Formation is at least 7,700 feet thick; the Elena is lithologically similar to the Chainman Shale and Diamond Peak Formation (Cornwall, 1972).
rocktype3: siltstone; sandstone; conglomerate; dolostone (dolomite); chert; quartzite
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV003 NV006 NV007 NV008 NV010 NV011 NV013

unitdesc: MASSIVE LIMESTONE-In the San Antonio Mountains, western Nye County
unit_com: Northwest of Lime Mountain, this unit consists only of limestone; southwest of Lime Mountain, this unit consists of primarily limestone with lesser limestone-cobble conglomerate and minor quartzitic sandstone and siliceous to calcitic argillite (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985).

unitdesc: SILICEOUS AND VOLCANIC ROCKS-In Humboldt County, consists of altered pillow lavas, coarse volcanic breccias, clastic limestone, and minor amounts of sandstone, shale, siliceous shale, and chert of the Goughs Canyon Formation (Lower and Upper Mississippian). In the East Range, Pershing County, consists of quartzite, conglomerate, slate, limestone, chert, and greenstone of the Inskip Formation (Mississippian?).
unit_com: In Humboldt County, this unit is composed of 70% altered volcanic rocks, 25% limestone, and 5% calcareous sandstone and shale, siliceous shale and chert; here it is about 5,000 feet thick (Willden, 1964). The Inskip Formation has been locally metamorphosed to phyllite and amphibolite; it is upto 9,000 feet thick (Johnson, 1977). Johnson, 1977, does not report greenstone or any altered or unaltered extrusive rock in the Inskip.
rocktype3: siltstone; limestone; shale; chert; conglomerate; quartzite

unitdesc: GRANITIC ROCKS, WESTERN NEVADA (Mesozoic)-Mostly quartz monzonite and granodiorite. Inconclusively dated or not dated radiometrically
unit_com: This unit is often grouped with rocks in unit NVKgr in the literature. Bonham, 1969, reports that while most of the intrusive bodies have the dimensions of stocks, it is commonly believed that the Mesozoic rocks of western Nevada (which are almost entirely in this unit and NVKgr) are a continuation of the composite batholith of the Sierra Nevada. Granodiorite is more abundant than quartz monzonite in Humboldt and Washoe Counties; the opposite is true in southern Nevada. In Humboldt County, this group contains all quartz bearing pre-late Tertiary intrusive rocks. This unit may also include aplite dikes, an alaskite body inclosed in granodiorite, and pegmatite not mapped at this scale (Willden, 1964, Bonham, 1969).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV005 NV009 NV012 NV016 NV017 NV019 NV020

unitdesc: LIMESTONE, DOLOMITE, SHALE, AND QUARTZITE-Includes units such as Pogonip Group, Eureka Quartzite, and Ely Springs Dolomite. Where Ely Springs Dolomite or equivalent rocks are included in SOc unit, this unit includes only the Pogonip Group and Eureka Quartzite or their equivalents.
strat_unit: Fish Haven Dolomite (Ely Springs Dolomite and the Hanson Creek Formation equivalent)?Hales Limestone (in part), Stoneberger Shale (Ninemile Formation of the Pogonip equivalent), Fish Haven Dolomite (Ely Springs Dolomite and the Hanson Creek Formation equivalent)?
unit_com: The Pogonip Group, Eureka Quartzite, and Ely Springs Dolomite have a combined thickness of 3,500 to 4,700 feet thick, thinning southward, with the Pogonip ranging 60 to 85% of that, the Eureka Quartzite ranging from almost 0 to 11%, and the Ely Springs Dolomite ranging from 8 to 30% (Longwell and others, 1965, Tschanz and Pampeyan, 1970, Hose and Blake, 1976). The Eureka Quartzite is a distinctive white band compared to the dark limestone and dolostone of the other two units. The Pogonip Group is made up three members corresponding to the Goodwin Formation, the Ninemile Formation, and the Antelope Valley Limestone, lower to upper respectively; however, the Pogonip has been divided into as many as nine different members (Longwell and others, 1965, Tschanz and Pampeyan, 1970). The Ely Springs Dolomite just contains the Silurian-Ordovician boundary (hence inclusion in unit NVSOC, particularly in White Pine County) (Longwell and others, 1965, Hose and Blake, 1976). Includes "post-Dunderberg Shale" Cambrian limestone in White Pine County (Hose and Blake, 1976).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV003 NV007 NV008 NV011

unitdesc: DOLOMITE AND LIMESTONE-Undivided Cambrian and Ordovician rocks in part of Clark County; mostly Cambrian.
strat_unit: Goodsprings Dolomite
unit_com: Unit occurs in Clark County only. The Goodsprings Dolomite is 2,500-3000+ feet thick; dolomitic limestone and sandy shale make up only the top 50 to 75 feet of this. The Goodsprings Dolomite has been divided into two units, the upper one called the Cornfield Springs Formation and the lower one called the Bonanza King Formation, mapped here in unit NVCc. The correlation between the Goodsprings Formation and the Bonanza King Formation is based on the stratigraphic position of Dunderberg fauna within the Goodsprings (the Dunderberg Shale overlies the Bonanza King Formation in unit NVCc). (Longwell and others, 1965).

unitdesc: SHALE AND CHERT-Includes Fourmile Canyon Formation in Eureka County and Noh Formation of Riva (1970) and unnamed rocks in Elko County.
unit_com: The Noh Formation is a shale, siltstone, chert, and sandstone unit unconformably overlying the Agort Chert (see unit NVOs); thickness is 325 to 1,100 feet (Coats, 1987). Silurian rocks of the western assemblage are mostly shale, siliceous shale, calcareous shale, and a few limestone beds; the Fourmile Canyon Formation has been mapped as interbedded chert, shale and silty sandstone (Roberts and others, 1967).

unitdesc: PHYLLITE, SHALE, AND LIMESTONE-Locally includes chert and quartzite. Includes Tennessee Mountain Formation of Bushnell (1967) in western Elko County, Broad Canyon sequence of Means (1962) in Lander County, and rocks originally mapped as Palmetto Formation in Toiyabe and Toquima Ranges, northern Nye County
strat_unit: Crane Canyon sequence (in Nye County), Van Duzer Limestone (in part), Pogonip Group (in small part), Tennessee Mountain Formation, Broad Canyon sequence
unit_com: In Nye County, includes slightly metamorphosed shale, mudstone, limestone, chert, and greenstone; phyllite, schist, argillite, and slate predominate over other strata (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). The Broad Canyon Sequence of Lander County consists of shale (slate), phyllite, argillite and limestone (marble) (Stewart and McKee, 1977). Tennessee Mountain Formation is approximately half phyllite and half limestone (Coats, 1987). Coats maps part of this unit as the Upper Paleozoic Van Duzer Limestone on the basis that these rocks resemble the Van Duzer in lithology, appearance, and vicinity (see also NVPMc). The Pogonip Group consists of what formally was known as the Eastside sequence; the Palmetto Formation consists of what was formally called the Manhatten sequence and included the Mayflower Schist, Zanzibar Limestone and Toquima Formation (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985).

unit_name: Shale, chert, and minor amounts of quartzite, greenstone, and limestone
unitdesc: SHALE, CHERT, AND MINOR AMOUNTS OF QUARTZITE, GREENSTONE, AND LIMESTONE-Includes units such as Vinini Formation of north-central Nevada, Palmetto Formation in southern and central parts of Esmeralda County, and Comus Formation in Humboldt County. Locally includes rocks of Silurian and Devonian age.
strat_unit: Clipper Canyon sequence, Valder Formation, Agort Chert, Basco Formation
unit_com: Shale and siltstone in the Palmetto Formation have locally been metamorphosed to hornfels (Albers and Stewart, 1972). The Comus Formation is approximately 25% limestone, 40% dolomite, and 35% shale; it ranges from 3,000 to 5,450 feet thick but makes up only an incidental part of this unit (Willden, 1964). A small portion of the Palmetto Formation in Esmeralda County has been assigned to NVOsv (Albers and Stewart, 1972).
rocktype3: limestone; quartzite; andesite; siltstone; sandstone; chemical; greenstone; dolostone (dolomite)
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV005 NV008 NV009 NV013

unitdesc: SILICEOUS AND VOLCANIC ROCKS-Chert, shale, quartzite, greenstone, and minor amounts of limestone. Includes units such as Valmy Formation of north-central Nevada and some rocks mapped as Palmetto Formation in northern part of Esmeralda County and adjacent parts of Mineral and Nye Counties. Locally includes rocks of Silurian and Devonian age.
strat_unit: McAfee Quartzite, Jacks Peak Formation, Snow Canyon Formation (all part of "Valmy Group"), Sonoma Range Formation, Palmetto Formation (in small part)
unit_com: Similar in lithology to NVOs but has larger proportion of volcanics and chert. The Sonoma Range Formation is overlain by the Valmy Formation and possibly correlative with the lower part of the Valmy; it is over 3,000 feet thick but limited to Humboldt County and possibly Pershing County (Willden, 1964, Johnson, 1977). The Valmy Formation occurs in thrust sheets but has been measured at a thickness of 8,000 feet and estimated to be 20,000 to 25,000 feet thick (Stewart and McKee, 1977).
rocktype3: shale; greenstone; limestone; conglomerate; siltstone; chemical
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV005 NV008 NV009 NV010 NV016

unitdesc: SHALE, CHERT, AND LIMESTONE-Includes Aura Formation of Decker (1962) in northwest Elko County and Perkins Canyon Formation of Kay and Crawford (1964) in northern Nye County
unit_com: The Aura Formation is primarily phyllite (included with shale in the lithology), partly calcareous, with chert and quartzite; its total thickness is 3,800 feet (Coats, 1987). The Perkins Canyon Formation includes shales and limestones (argillicalcilutite interbedded with black shaly argillites) (Kay and Crawford, 1964).

unitdesc: LIMESTONE-Includes Ely Limestone (mostly Lower and Middle Pennsylvanian)
unit_com: LIMITED TO OUTCROPS IN NORTHERN NYE AND EUREKA COUNTIES. The maximum thickness of the Ely Limestone in Eureka County is 1,500 feet. Clastic beds generally become more abundant in the Ely Limestone northward from Eureka (these lithologies are included in NVPPPc) (Roberts and others, 1967).

unit_name: Limestone, cherty limestone, sandy limestone, and chert-pebble conglomerate
unitdesc: LIMESTONE, CHERTY LIMESTONE, SANDY LIMESTONE, AND CHERT-PEBBLE CONGLOMERATE (Lower and Middle Pennsylvanian)-Includes units such as Moleen and Tomera Formations of Dott (1955)
strat_unit: Ely Limestone (in small part)
unit_com: The outcrops in northern Nye County are Ely Limestone (see also NVPPc, and NVPPPc). The Moleen and Tomera Formations range from 1,200 to 1,600 feet thick. Coats, 1987, mapped the outcrops in northern Elko County (near Mary River Peak) with units mapped here in NVPMc.

unit_name: Platy limestone and limy siltstone, chert at base
unitdesc: PLATY LIMESTONE AND LIMY SILTSTONE, CHERT AT BASE-Includes units such as Roberts Mountains Formation, and Storff Formation and Chellis Limestone of Decker (1962). Locally includes rocks of Early Devonian age at top.
strat_unit: Chellis Limestone, Storff Formation, Roberts Mountains Formation
unit_com: The Chellis Limestone is 1,900 feet thick and the Storff Formation is 3,900 feet thick; both formations are limited to northern Elko County (Coats, 1987). The Roberts Mountains Formation makes up the rest of this unit and ranges from 500 to 1,700 feet thick (Roberts and others, 1967, Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985, Stewart and McKee, 1977). The Roberts Mountains Formation includes calcisiltite and calcilutite (Coats, 1987), and silty limestone (Stewart and McKee, 1977), all of which was classified as limestone, rather than siltstone, in the lithology coding.
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV008 NV010 NV013

unit_name: Cherty limestone and sparse dolomite, shale, and sandstone
unitdesc: CHERTY LIMESTONE AND SPARSE DOLOMITE, SHALE, AND SANDSTONE (Lower and Upper Permian)-Includes units such as Park City Group and equivalent rocks in northern Nevada and Toroweap Formation and Kaibab Limestone in southern Nevada
strat_unit: Phosphoria Formation (including Meade Peak Phosphoratic Shale and Rex Chert), Gerster Limestone, Murdock Mountain Formation, Grandeur Formation, Plympton Formation
unit_com: All of the stratigraphic units included, except for the Phosphoria, are part of the Park City Group and occur in Elko and White Pine County; the Kaibab Limestone is also considered part of the Park City Group but occurs mostly in Lincoln and Clark Counties along with the Toroweap. Note that the Grandeur Formation is equivalent to the Kaibab Limestone. Coats, 1987, mapped parts of the Park City Group with the Pequop Formation in Elko County (see NVPsc); what is mapped as Park City Group is mostly dolomite (rather than limestone). In Elko County, this unit appears to range from about 650 to 2,000 feet thick. The Gerster Formation has been described locally as dolomitic and calcareous siltstone with chert but is regionally described as a cherty, bioclastic limestone (Coats, 1987). The Kaibab and Toroweap Formations in Lincoln County range from 240 to 450 feet thick; these rocks are not widespread however (Tschanz and Pampeyan, 1970). Relative proportions of carbonate and clastic rocks varies throughout unit; carbonate rocks appear to total a larger percentage than clastic rocks.
rocktype3: dolostone (dolomite); sandstone; siltstone; chert; conglomerate; phosphorite; evaporite
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV003 NV007 NV008 NV011

unitdesc: LIMESTONE, DOLOMITE, AND SHALE (Upper Paleozoic)-Includes Van Duzer Limestone of Decker (1962)
strat_unit: Poorman Peak Formation, Hammond Canyon Formation, Oquirrh Formation?
unit_com: The Van Duzer Limestone is more than 7,200 feet thick but is limited to one large outcrop in Bull Run Quadrangle. See NVOCt for the other rocks in the area which resemble the Van Duzer Limestone. The remainder of this unit is described by Coats, 1987, as "the unit of limestone, shale, chert, orthoquartzite, and quartz siltite". It includes the Poorman Peak and Hammond Creek Formations as well as outcrops too faulted to be divided into formations. Thicknesses range from 1,800 to 4,300 feet thick. Coats, 1987, does not include dolomite in this unit.

unit_name: Havallah sequence of Silberling and Roberts (1962)
unitdesc: HAVALLAH SEQUENCE OF SILBERLING AND ROBERTS (1962)-Chert, argillite, shale, greenstone, and minor amounts of siltstone, sandstone, conglomerate, and limestone. Includes Schoonover Formation of Fagan (1962) and Reservation Hill Formation in Elko County, Farrel Canyon Formation in southwestern Humboldt County, Havallah and Pumpernickel Formations in Pershing, Lander, and parts of Humboldt Counties, and rocks originally considered a part of the Pablo and Excelsior Formations in northern Nye, northern Esmeralda, and southern Mineral Counties. Assignment of some rocks to the Havallah sequence in the East Range, Pershing County, is highly uncertain. Includes rocks ranging in age from Late Mississippian to Early Permian
unit_com: The estimated thickness of the Excelsior Formation is 10,000 feet (Ross, 1961). The thickness of the Havallah-Pumpernickel sequence in Pershing County is 15,000 to 17,000 feet thick if the Pumpernickel-like rocks lie both above and below the Havallah rocks or is 12,000 to 14,000 feet thick if these rocks are superimposed structurally (Johnson, 1977). The greenstone and volcanic rocks of the Pumpernickel are more abundant in western outcrops where they can constitute as much as 20% of the unit; in the eastern outcrops, the greenstone occurs only incidentally (Stewart and McKee, 1977). Stewart and McKee, 1977, report that the total thickness of the Havallah is estimated to be about 10,000 feet thick and of the Pumpernickel to be 5,000 feet thick. Very often, the Pumpernickel and Havallah are mapped as one unit, undifferentiated. The Pablo Formation in northern Nye County has undergone regional metamorphism, consisting of pelitic rocks, slate, hornfels, chert, and basaltic rocks (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). According to Coats, 1987, the Reservation Hill Formation is assigned to this unit because it is convenient to do so in the lack of established correlation to any other Paleozoic rocks of Nevada.
unit_ref: NV001 NV004 NV005 NV008 NV009 NV012 NV013 NV017

unit_name: Antler Sequence of Silberling and Roberts (1962)
unitdesc: ANTLER SEQUENCE OF SILBERLING AND ROBERTS (1962) (Middle Pennsylvanian to Early or Late Permian) (Guadalupian)-Conglomerate, sandy to conglomeratic limestone, limestone, sandstone, and calcareous shale. Thin detrital and carbonate sequence within main part of Antler orogenic belt. Includes units such as Sunflower Formation of Bushnell (1967) in Elko County, Battle Formation, Antler Peak Limestone, and Edna Mountain Formation in Lander and western Eureka Counties, and Wildcat Peak Formation in northern Nye County
strat_unit: Highway Limestone
unit_com: The Wildcat Formation is 50 to 164 feet of limestone overlain by 868 of conglomerate (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). The Brock Canyon Formation is about 4,900 feet thick, of which 6-15% is conglomerate, 15-20% is quartzite and dolomite, 38% is claystone and siltstone, and 33% is arkose (Roberts and others, 1967). The Battle Formation ranges from 50-730 feet thick; it is mostly conglomerate with minor shale, sandstone, and limestone. The Antler Peak Limestone is 100 to 800 feet thick. The Edna Mountain Formation in Lander County is about 200 feet thick; it is mostly shale and limestone with some conglomerate (Stewart and McKee, 1977). In Humboldt County, the Edna Mountain Formation is mostly sandstone with some slate, quartzite, limestone, and conglomerate, and ranges from 200 to 300 feet thick. The Highway Limestone is equivalent to the upper part of the Battle Formation as mapped at its type locality; it is also difficult to distinguish from the Antler Peak Limestone except by fauna and where the two units are separated by a thin bed of conglomerate (Willden, 1964). The Sunflower Formation is over 4,000 feet thick, of which 47% is conglomerate, 13% limestone, and 35% sandstone. This unit also includes sandstone and siltstone on Horse Mountain with a thickness of 800 feet (Coats, 1987).
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV004 NV005 NV008 NV010 NV013

unit_name: Limestone and sparse dolomite, siltstone, and sandstone
unitdesc: LIMESTONE AND SPARSE DOLOMITE, SILTSTONE, AND SANDSTONE-Includes units such as undivided Riepe Spring Limestone of Steele (1960) and Ely Limestone or their equivalent in Elko, White Pine, and northern Lincoln Counties and most of the Bird Spring Formation and Callville Limestone in Clark and southern Lincoln Counties. Includes some stratigraphically higher Permian rocks in Leppy Peak, easternmost Elko County.
strat_unit: Tippipah Limestone, Pakoon Limestone, Bluepoint Limestone, Hogan Formation, Ferguson Mountain Formation, Rib Hill Formation (in part), Strathearn Formation (in part)
unit_com: TAGGED AS PPC IN DIGITAL COVERAGE. The Tippipah Limestone in southern Nye County (may also be mapped as the Bird Spring Formation) is 3,600 feet thick (Cornwall, 1972). The Pakoon Limestone has been mapped as the upper part of the Callville Formation by some geologists; the Bluepoint Limestone is included in the basal part of the Calville. Measured and estimated thicknesses for the Bird Spring Limestone range from 2,500 to 7,000 feet (Longwell and others, 1965), though Tschanz and Pampeyan report that the Bird Spring Formation in the Mormon Mountains in Lincoln County may be no thicker than 1,000 feet; elsewhere in Lincoln County, Pennsylvanian rocks measure up to 3,500 feet. The thickness of the Ely and Riepe Spring Limestones range from 1,500 to 2,950 (Hose and Blake, 1976). Coats, 1987, includes the Hogan Formation within the Ely Limestone.
unit_ref: NV001 NV002 NV003 NV006 NV007 NV008 NV011

unit_name: Siltstone, sandstone, limestone, and dolomite (commonly silty or sandy) and gypsum
unitdesc: SILTSTONE, SANDSTONE, LIMESTONE, AND DOLOMITE (COMMONLY SILTY OR SANDY), AND GYPSUM (Lower Permian)-Includes units such as Rib Hill Sandstone and Pequop Formation of Steele (1959) in Elko County, Rib Hill Sandstone and Arcturus Formation in White Pine County, Queantoweap Sandstone of NcNair (1951), Hermit Shale, and Coconino Sandstone in Clark and southern Lincoln Counties.
strat_unit: Loray Formation
unit_com: The Pequop Formation is a 1,500 to 5,200 foot section of fusulinid limestone with a basal red silt member; the Loray Formation overlies it and may be mapped with both the Pequop Formation and the Park City Group (see NVPc) (Coats, 1987). The Rib Hill Sandstone ranges from 470 to 1,400 feet thick, depending on the interpreted position of the contact between it and the Arcturus (Hose and Blake, 1976). Hose and Blake, 1976, include the Loray of Clark County with the Arcturus. The red beds overlying the Callville Limestone in Clark County are questionably correlative to the Supai Formation of the Colorado Plateau. The red beds are 1,100 to 1,200 feet thick and have been divided into the Hermit Shale and Queantoweap Sandstone by McNair (Longwell and others, 1965). This unit may include Callville Limestone (see NVPPPc).

unitdesc: SEDIMENTARY ROCKS-Mostly lake deposits
unit_com: The largest outcrop (and majority of this unit) is in Eureka County. Named the Hay Ranch Formation by Regnier (1960), it consists of lake deposits of clay, vitric tuff (mostly altered to zeolites), limestones, and tan tuffaceous siltstones and sandstones with interfingering conglomerates. It is overlain by pediment and outcrops are present mostly around tributaries of Pine Creek. Other minor outcrops of this unit in southwest Nevada consist of weakly consolidated or bedded sediments ranging from gravel to clay.

unitdesc: DOLOMITE-Includes units such as Laketown and Lone Mountain Dolomites. Locally includes rocks of Early Devonian age at top.
strat_unit: Nevada Formation (in part?); Sevy Dolomite (in part)
unit_com: The Lone Mountain Dolomite ranges from 1,570 to 3,200 feet thick. The Lone Mountain Dolomite is laterally equivalent to the Robert Mountains Formation (see unit NVSt) (Roberts and others, 1967). The Laketown Dolomite outcrops in Nye and Lincoln Counties and ranges from 0 to 1000 feet in thickness (Tschanz and Pampeyan, 1970, Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). In southern Elko County, there is an outcrop which consists of Fish Haven Dolomite (Ordovician--see unit NVOc and NVSOc), the Laketown Dolomite, and the Sevy Dolomite (Devonian, see unit NVDc), undifferentiated. The Sevy Dolomite also overlies the Lone Mountain Formation in Clark County and just a part of it is included in this unit (Longwell and others, 1965). Similarly, the Nevada Formation (which is almost entirely limestone and dolostone and is Devonian in age) lies stratigraphically above the Lone Mountain Dolomite in Eureka County (Roberts and others, 1967) and stratigraphically above the Laketown Dolomite in northern Nye County (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985); in both cases, just a part of the Nevada appears to be included in this unit.

unitdesc: ELDER SANDSTONE-Feldspathic sandstone, siltstone, shale, and chert. Lander County.
unit_com: The Elder Sandstone is at least 2,000 feet thick and probably more than 4,000 feet thick (Stewart and McKee, 1977).

unitdesc: DOLOMITE-Includes uppermost part of Ordovician System (Ely Springs Dolomite and equivalent rocks) and all of Silurian System.
strat_unit: Fish Haven Dolomite (Ely Springs Dolomite and Hanson Creek Formation equivilent), Laketown Dolomite (in part)
unit_com: The Ely Springs Dolomite is included in White Pine County, parts of Elko County (Hose and Blake, 1976, Coats, 1987). Thickness of Ely Springs Dolomite and Laketown Dolomite in the Egan Range is 2,050 feet. Quartzite interbeds with the dolomite at the contact with the underlying Eureka Quartzite (see unit NVOc). There is one bed no more than 10 feet thick of quartizitic chert in the Laketown Dolomite (Hose and Blake, 1976). Locally includes some Sevy Dolomite in Elko County (see unit NVDc) (Coats, 1987).

unitdesc: LIMESTONE, MINOR AMOUNTS OF DOLOMITE, SHALE, AND SANDSTONE; LOCALLY THICK CONGLOMERATE UNITS (Lower, Middle, and Upper Triassic)-Includes Tobin, Dixie Valley, Favret, Augusta Mountain, and Cane Spring Formations and Star Peak Group in central Nevada and Grantsville and Luning Formations in west-central Nevada
strat_unit: Prida Formation, Natchez Pass Formation (both of the Star Peak Group)
unit_com: This unit also contains some of the Gabbs and Sunrise Formations (see NVJTRs) where undivided from the Luning Formation in northern Nye County (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). The Luning Formation ranges from 3000 to 10,000 feet thick (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985, Ross, 1961). The Tobin (900 feet thick), Dixie Valley (150 to 800 feet thick), and Favret (700 feet thick) Formations are correlative with the lower and middle members of the Prida Formation (400 to 2,500 feet thick); the Augusta Formation (2,500 feet thick) is stratigraphically correlative with the upper member of the Prida and the lower member of the Natchez Formation (1,650 to 2,500 feet thick; the Cane Spring Formation (1,000 to 1,500 feet thick) is equivalent to the upper member of the Natchez (Johnson, 1977).

unitdesc: CHINLE FORMATION AND ASSOCIATED ROCKS (Upper Triassic)-Continental deposits of variegated bentonitic claystone, siltstone, and clayey sandstone; ledge-forming sandstone; and red siltstone
unit_com: Primarily located in Clark County and southern Lincoln County; one outcrop in Elko County which could be correlative with the Chinle Formation as well as the Timothy Sandstone and Nugget Sandstone. The measured thickness of the Chinle Formation ranges from 750 to 3,300 feet (Longwell and others, 1965). The relative abundances of shale, siltsone, and sandstone are unspecified in referenced literture; the ranking of each of these units is speculative.

Includes Tallman Fanglomerate (Permian?) in Humboldt County

unit_name: Conglomerate, sandstone, shale, and dolomite of Diablo Formation below and shale, sandstone, and conglomerate of Candelaria Formation above
unitdesc: CONGLOMERATE, SANDSTONE, SHALE, AND DOLOMITE OF DIABLO FORMATION BELOW AND SHALE, SANDSTONE, AND CONGLOMERATE OF CANDELARIA FORMATION ABOVE (Lower or Upper Permian to Lower Triassic)-Mineral, Esmeralda, and northwestern Nye Counties
unit_com: In Mineral and Esmeralda Counties, the Diablo Formation ranges from 200 to 400 feet thick and is chiefly composed of sandstone and grit and dolomite, the relative proportions of which vary locally (Ross, 1961, Albers and Stewart, 1972); in northern Nye County, the Diablo Formation ranges anywhere from 131 feet to 3,280 feet thick and is composed of siltstone interbedded with conglomerate, sandstone, grit, and limestone (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). In Mineral and Esmeralda Counties, the Candelaria Formation is 3,200 feet thick and composed of shale with lesser to equal amounts of sandstone and minor limestone and conglomerate (Ross, 1961, Albers and Stewart, 1972); in northern Nye County, the Candelaria Formation at Willow Spring is reported to be mostly argillite and siltite with minor limestone and quartzite (Kleinhampl and Ziony, 1985). Argillite is included with siltstone in the lithology coding.

unit_name: Silty limestone, minor amounts of shale, and some greenstone
unitdesc: SILTY LIMESTONE, MINOR AMOUNTS OF SHALE, AND SOME GREENSTONE-Unnamed sequence in Adobe Range, northern Elko County
strat_unit: Long Canyon sequence
unit_com: The thickness of this unit is estimated at over 2000 feet. All three rock types occur in both the Triassic and Permian sections; the volcanic rocks form resistant beds a few feet thick concordent with enclosing sedimentary beds (Coats, 1987). Coats (1987) says only that there are intermediate-composition volcanic rocks present; Ketner (1975) identifies the volcanic rocks as greenstone.

unit_name: Volcanic flows and flow breccias, chiefly of andesitic composition, tuffs, sparse sandstone and graywacke
unitdesc: VOLCANIC FLOWS AND FLOW BRECCIAS, CHIEFLY OF ANDESITIC COMPOSITION, TUFFS, SPARSE SANDSTONE AND GRAYWACKE-Includes Happy Creek Volcanic Series and related rocks in Humboldt County and similar rocks in Washoe and Pershing Counties; includes andesite breccias and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks in Mineral County
strat_unit: Excelsior Formation (in part); Dunlap Formation (in part)
unit_com: The composition of the Happy Creek volcanic series ranges from andesitic to basaltic, with andesite being more abundant (Willden, 1964). Rocks in northwestern Pershing County are both andesitic and dacitic in composition and have undergone lower greenschist, amphibolite, or hornfels facies metamorphism (Johnson, 1977). All sedimentary rocks occur associated with volcanic rocks of certain areas: the limestone and conglomerate with rocks of Washoe County (Bonham, 1969), the limy shale (limestone?) and chert with rocks of Pershing County (Johnson, 1977), sandstone, conglomerate and calcareous rocks with the Dunlap (Ross, 1961), and the graywacke and sandstone with the Happy Creek volcanic series (Willden, 1964).

unitdesc: QUARTZITE, PHYLLITIC SILTSTONE, CONGLOMERATE, LIMESTONE, AND DOLOMITE-Includes McCoy Creek Group (excluding Stella Lake Quartzite) in east-central Nevada and Johnnie Formation in southern Nevada.
unit_com: Johnnie Formation is 4200-4500 feet thick (Longwell and others, 1965). The McCoy Creek Group is over 9,000 feet thick (Hose and Blake, 1976). The McCoy Creek Group is slightly metamorphosed to argillite, slate, phyllite, and marble. Also includes small outcrops, not of the McCoy Group, of sillimanite-biotite schist and quartzitic schist in Elko County (Coats, 1987). I did not find limestone reported in any of the county maps.

unitdesc: WYMAN FORMATION-Phyllite and phyllitic siltstone and minor amounts of limestone, dolomite, and sandstone
unit_com: Albers and Stewart, 1972, describe the Wyman Formation as primarily siltstone with thin limestone interbeds; the strata are somewhat metamorphosed and commonly grade to phyllite, schist, marble, and calc-silicate and siliceous hornfels. In Nevada, the Wyman Formation is 960-1350 feet thick, while in the White-Inyo Range, the Formation is 9,000+ feet thick; in neither location is the base exposed.
